utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any preliminary matters? Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I just wanted to use the opportunity to say that the next witness, Radojca Mladjenovic, would require more than 30 minutes that we had originally asked for. Therefore, we would kindly ask your indulgence to grant us 45 minutes to examine that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that, Mr. Stojanovic. But let me just have a look. I have Mladjenovic not as the next witness. I have Mr. Ujic as the next witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. The witness who comes after Mr. Ujic is Mr. Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then clear. We'll consider it. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just since we're addressing time matters, I'm still going to try to do my cross-examination on the current witness in two and a half hours. However, I did review. Since there was one associated exhibit that was not tendered yesterday, I may need to put some other things into the record which might carry me slightly over and I just want to alert the Chamber as to that since I had anticipated that that associated exhibit was going to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But I'm still going to try to maintain my time estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom? I think the usher is already trying to find him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, and I would also like to remind you that you do not appear as a teacher -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear you. Can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear very well. Can you put up the sound?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll be assisted. Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I repeat what I said, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And I would also like to remind you that yesterday I made a few observations about your role in this courtroom; that is, not a professor, a teacher, a person who gives exegesis of texts written by others, but that we expect you to give us the information on matters you've observed yourself, you heard, you've seen, et cetera, rather than more general observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination-in-chief. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday we left off talking about your encounters with General Mladic. I would like to ask you based upon these encounters, your observations and knowledge of General Mladic, and your military background, how would you assess his attitude towards warfare and the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less all of us, including General Mladic, fosters military values and was raised on traditional Serbian officers. I have never heard anything bad about the enemy side from General Mladic, nothing defamatory, nothing derogatory. I personally believe that his experience of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was very difficult. But he had to place himself at the head of the Serbian army in order to avoid a repetition of the past which was not glorious. General Mladic acquired those values that I would like to share with you. If the Trial Chamber will allow me, I would like to tell you what are the values of a Serbian general and a Serbian officer. I believe that he is a rare --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that goes beyond the question, to tell us what -- you were asked for an impression on the basis of your personal encounters with General Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based on your encounters with General Mladic, which particular values did he seem to embody?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general is a very capable man, very energetic man, very modest man. He never asked for any privileges in his life while he was in command of the Serbian army. He never enjoyed any special treatment. The proof of that is that he ate the same food as everybody else. He visited the troops whenever he could, the troops on positions. He imparted fatherly advice. I observed all that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last sentence of your answer as the interpreters did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed all that when I met with General Mladic, what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in terms of the values that seemed to be embodied and expressed by General Mladic, could you tell us a little bit more about his attitude towards the opposing side, the enemy side? How did he treat them?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about the relationship between General Mladic and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and his attitude and his -- and what he told the Sarajevo Romanija Corps about the enemy side. The most important thing is this: There was never a suggestion that only the Muslim territory should be attacked, the settlements populated be the Muslim population. An example for that is Butmir and Hrasnica. Those settlements are inhabited predominantly by a Muslim population. When I visited Famos in 1993 and Famos was on the line of contact with Hrasnica and Muslim positions, the general manager, Berijan [phoen], who is now unfortunately is deceased, told me that they had allegedly visited General Mladic and asked him to launch an attack to repel Muslims a bit further away from Famos. On that occasion, General Mladic said that it would never occurred to him to do that because it was their territory. And now in hindsight I would say that that was an exceptionally fair decision. And this shows that the respect for the Muslim population in that area was never an issue. As far as the other aspects of the work of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps are concerned, General Mladic trusted the corps and its commanders. He knew that the Serbian population from Vogosca to Ilidza and Hadzici or Vojkovici and all the villages at the foot of Trebevic were doing nothing else but defending their own households, their own land, and that's all. Nothing else. He knew that that was the biggest motive of their fight, to protect those villages. General Mladic on two occasions assisted the corps the first time and the second time when he made sure that some companies arrived from Krajina to man the combat positions on the Vogosca-Rajlovac axis. That was of a short duration. Otherwise, he had full trust in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and its combat capabilities. And another thing that I would like to say about General Mladic. There was a prevalent opinion that he was not well disposed towards General Milosevic. On one occasion, General Milosevic invited me to his office and he showed me the official grade written on his behalf by General Mladic. The grade that General Mladic gave to General Milosevic contained some 20 elements. General Mladic gave General Milosevic all fives. He gave him only one grade four. And General Milosevic said he was delighted when he said that -- he said that General Mladic obviously respected everything that General Milosevic was doing in his effort to preserve the Serbian territories in the Sarajevo sector. In other words, it is not true. Those were just rumours that there was any love lost between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you skillfully circumvented my effort to get the witness back to the question and to his personal observations. I've now listened for five minutes where the witness dealt with a lot of matters which are totally unrelated to the question. If you want this Chamber to take your request for time seriously, then please keep better control of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question for clarification, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't mind. Sir, at page 5, line 9, you said or you're recorded as saying: "There was never a suggestion that only the Muslim territory would be attacked." Now, my question to you is: Which other ethnic territory did he say must be attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No territories were ever attacked, not even outside of the zone of Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I'm not aware of that. But he respected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did you mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the territories of which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. You've answered my question. You've answered my question. Thank you so much. What did you mean by not only the Muslim territories would be attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you have misspoken, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the territories inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could return to D686 MFI, and page 2 in the Serbian and page 2 to 3 in the English, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk of the advantage of the ABiH 2.5 or 3:1 over the SRK. Given your military training and given the odds, was it ever even feasible for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to try to take over Sarajevo militarily?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, when cities are being conquered, the ratio of forces should be 3:1. In other words, the attacker has to have the strength three times greater than the defence. In this case, this was not the case. Therefore, there was no reason. There was not any indication that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps would launch an attack and commit suicide in that way. Fire from Sarajevo did not have to be open on our positions, and then we returned fire and there was a lot of collateral damage. In other words, the initiative was in the hands of the 1st Corps which was prevalent and its troops were better rested and in a better shape than the troops of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to paragraph 8, which is on the same page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk of Muslim propaganda to portray Sarajevo as St. Petersburg. What more can you tell us about your personal observations in this regard dating from the time in your detention at hotel Europa?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the 3rd May onwards. I heard on the radio, there was a lot of propaganda that in Dobrinja Serbs had killed 17 children. While I was in Europa hotel, I recorded 42 explosions in the space of one hour on a rock above Bistrik. I recorded all those on a map, 42 explosions. They should have portrayed the situation as Sarajevo having been under a constant cannonade of Serbian forces. The objective of the propaganda was to tarnish the enemy side as much as possible, to boost the combat readiness of its own forces, to engage the -- their own people to support their forces, to make the recruitment efforts easier. In any case, there was a lot of propaganda about Serbs who cut off Muslim hands and then played football with them. And there was another thing that is something that is commonly heard in wars, that fingers are made into necklaces, and so on and so forth. I had a personal encounter in Europa hotel with a high representative of Muslims who happened to be there. I would like his name to be protected, Mr. President. I will tell you who he was but I don't want to say that in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does this relate to my question as to your personal observations of efforts of propaganda to portray Sarajevo as St. Petersburg?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the city was encircled, which it wasn't. I studied the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's -- let's go back.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the blockade of Leningrad, but Sarajevo had absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with Leningrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are pressed for time. I want you to please clarify for us. When you say 42 explosions were -- were those explosions on the same rock? Were they in a different area? I don't understand your answer in that regard. Could you please explain that for us.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see that all of those explosions happened in the same place. Then I started plotting those places on a map and they repeated in the same place. There will be a cloud of dust and then an explosion, a cloud of dust and then an explosion. And it is very important for me to tell you about my meeting, and I would kindly ask you to go into private session because I don't want to say the person's name in open session. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that about the same high representative you -- that happened to be in the Europa hotel? Is that what you want to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any specific reason why that person could not be called by his name, if it's a he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was a businessman. He was the head of state of commodity reserves. I don't know whether he returned to Sarajevo or not. I don't know. But he was a high official. He informed my family ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He informed my family that I was being held hostage in hotel Europa, that man. But I wanted to say something else, Mr. President. We spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it one by one. You wanted to tell us about a meeting with this high representative. You asked for private session. We have listened to the reasons you have given and the Chamber finds no reason to hear that specific portion in private session. So please tell us about the meeting and tell us with whom you met.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not a meeting. I just happened to meet him in hotel Europa where he was because he couldn't go to his apartment. We spoke. He is an intellectual. And then he informed my family that I was being held hostage in hotel Europa. But this is what he told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But tell us first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]... gone -- he was the director of state commodity reserves, Ibro Prses. I have his business card. I'm sorry, I did not bring it from home. I can send it to you. And this is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us what this man -- how do you spell his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P, as in Pittsburgh, R as in Rostok, Ibro Prses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed. If it's relevant, it is about portraying Sarajevo as St. Petersburg. That was what the question was about. Could you tell us what, in that respect, he said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't speak to me about that. He told me something else which I believed to be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it relates in any way to any question Mr. Ivetic will put to you, then you may raise that. But at this moment that question was focused on propaganda portraying Sarajevo as St. Petersburg. Mr. Ivetic, I leave it in your hands how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to move to my next topic and then after that see, if we have time remaining, then we can return to this. But I would like to move to the next topic which I would like to explore with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But before you move to this other topic, I have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness Maksimovic, you said that you had a map where you plotted the location of explosions. From whom did you get this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not a map. I didn't have a map. I recorded the explosions on a simple piece of paper because I wasn't allowed to have anything else and later on I tore up this piece of paper and threw away the pencil, because I was a hostage. I was ready to condemned all of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stop you. I only asked about the map. You said on page 8 -- no, page 9, line 1: "I recorded all those on a map, 42 explosions." This is what you said. And later on you repeated that: "Then I started plotting those places on a map and they repeated in the same place." This is page 10, lines 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter may have misunderstood the witness and apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at this locations through my window. There was no map. There was just an ordinary piece of paper which I later tore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The -- it is clarified now because the interpreters may have misunderstood you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one very short question: Where exactly is hotel Europa located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Europa hotel is on the edges of the town, precisely between Bascarsija and Sarajevo downtown. And this hotel was donated by a Serb. His name was Jeftanovic and he was the one who built this hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the distance as the crow flies to Bistrik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, almost a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 800 to 900 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, if it assists, I don't think there is going to be much dispute about where hotel Europa is located. And I -- if it assists the Chamber we can find it on a map, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the parties agree with that, but in order to understand fully the testimony of the witness, of course, for us it would be important to know what he observed from where exactly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we may have already some evidence on the record from a protected witness as to the location of that hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be. I hope you'll forgive me for not having every single line in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was only reminded of it by my colleague as well, so I fall into the same boat as Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to move to another topic, sir. How were the relations with the Bosnian Croats, that is between the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska, in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to talk about what I was personally involved in and what I experienced. On the 10th or 11th of June, General Mladic sent me to Ilidza. I accepted unwillingly but I obeyed his order. He even offered me the post of the brigade commander, which I rejected since I was not an appropriate officer for that. I wasn't greedy to grab the post and then make some foolish mistake. When I arrived there on the 11th of July, I mean at Ilidza, I inspected the positions from Hadzici and Kiseljak leading to us. I had an encounter with an HVO representative. It happened accidentally in -- on the pass called Kobiljaca where the house was of another man. The HVO representative's last name was Bosnjak. We had a conversation and I told him that Kiseljak had never created problems for Serbs in Sarajevsko Polje and that they should continue in the same spirit and that we don't need to open a front line with them. I don't know how I would have faired if somebody from the higher command heard my statement. It doesn't mean that they heeded my advice but I had a very frank and sincere conversation with him. Further on concerning the relations between the HVO and the SRK, it's something that I didn't have any impact on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, the answer stands, I guess, now, but we did have an objection on the broadening of the scope of this topic based on the lack of notice previously. I let the initial thing go because we did say that we would be okay with the witness talking about his direct experience which he had been doing up until the last comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I don't think we have to -- an observation was made by Mr. Weber. If you do not disagree with him, you are invited to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the last comment that he's talking about that goes beyond the witness's personal knowledge. I'm not locating it in the transcript. So I'm a little bit confused by his comment, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I rose because when the witness started to say: "Further on concerning the relations between the HVO and the SRK ..." It appeared he was broadening from his experience to more general comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know yet whether he did or he did not. That's when you interrupted him. It could well be. It could also be that he would have stayed within the realm of his own observations. Mr. Ivetic, but you're reminded of what apparently seems to have been agreed upon between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know of no such agreement, Your Honour, with the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't -- you didn't contradict Mr. Weber yesterday when he said that he would allow you to continue as long as you stayed within the certain matters, and I thought that that was agreed. But, if not, there is no agreement and Mr. Weber will be on his feet whenever he thinks that it goes beyond --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He expects you to -- okay. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, I don't think we've gone beyond anything that was in the proofing statement. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm really confused by this because I believe that this was precisely put -- set forth in the proofing statement which was sent according to the same rules that the Prosecution used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So why do we have different rules? The Prosecution proofing noting was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The proofing note was sent in advance of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm now trying for a couple of lines to invite you to continue and we'll act as we see how the matter develops. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any personal involvement and personal knowledge of any other interactions with the Bosnian Croats and/or the HVO in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps during the course of your deployment during the war? And if so, could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So let us settle this: That was the only contact I had with the HVO at Kobiljaca. There were no other contacts. However, in November of 1993, following General Galic's order who was in Vogosca at the time with his staff, when the HVO commander from Kiseljak by the name of Rajic came seeking assistance from General Galic and permission for the Croatian population from Central Bosnia, that is to say between Kakanj, Kraljeva, Suceska, Breza, and Vares, to come to our territory - specifically Nisic Viseran [phoen] - General Galic probably had approval from General Mladic to accommodate the Croat's request, and then Rajic said that he needed a high-ranking officer in order to try to console the people who were frightened to go out and they were anxious. General Galic ordered me to go along with Rajic to the Nisic plateau, or rather towards Vares, and said that I should act as a guarantor that nothing would happen to the population. We went down to the village of Dastansko. The sight was terrible. People were terrified. It was extremely cold. There were several thousands of people from Vares and other places. They reached the Nisic plateau in the area of Okruglica village. Rajic and I -- or, rather, I asked Rajic to invite his battalion commanders so that I can converse with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take one step backwards. You still have not told us the circumstances that were in place why these people needed to be accommodated and why you had to go out there. What was going on that these people needed to be accommodated on SRK territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. Foundation. If it's directly related to this and he was personally told something, that's fine. If there is a foundation for it and he was informed of why in direct relation of this, fine. But the question is overly broad and there has been no foundation established as of yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if there is a risk of the witness going beyond his personal observation, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking you at this moment anything, Mr. Maksimovic. Could you phrase the question in such a way that that risk is limited as is possible in the present circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we could limit ourselves to your personal knowledge at that time - that is to say, when you went with Mr. Rajic to meet these people, these Bosnian Croat civilians - what was your personal knowledge of what was going on such that they had to be met by you and accommodated on SRK territory?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They quite simply fled the Muslim offensive that was being launched in the area and hence they crossed over to our territory. In other words, they abandoned Vares and other places due to the Muslim offensive and in fear of retaliation. This is what I directly knew and I know about it. They managed to withstand the offensive for a long time but ultimately they were defeated. They crossed over to our territory and the political leadership gave them permission. I was there to operationalise this decision and I acted as a person to whom the Croats can appeal if they had misunderstandings with someone else. Eventually they accepted that and they left to various places including to Serbia over Croatia. As far as I know, there were no problems relating to their evacuation across our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us, again based upon your personal knowledge and direct involvement, about what happened to the Bosnian Croat soldiers from these villages around Vares? What did they do? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They agreed to cover a 6-kilometre-long front line to fill in the gaps that they had made, and that we all prevent the approach of Muslims to the Nisic plateau. They remained at these positions for seven months until, I think, June of 1994. They had agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask a clarification you said in your response, "And that we all prevent the approach of Muslims." Who is the "we" in this scenario? Who was working together to prevent the approach of Muslims to say Nisic plateau?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were the Army of Republika Srpska and now we were reinforced by about 1200 Croats from their army who were holding these positions facing Selacke [phoen] mountain which was a gap because they were in Vares. Once they left Vares, it opened up a door for the Muslims to attack the Nisic plateau and we had to defend that because our survival depended on that. The Nisic "visoravan" was an extremely important feature in terms of operational issues. We kept it under our control the whole time because there was Serbian villages, Okruglica, Perkovici, Vacici [as interpreted], and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ship-of-the-line Captain Maksimovic, on behalf of my client and the rest of my team, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Maksimovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find Mr. Weber to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit D689 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, coming up will be a document associated to paragraph 70 of your statement. It is a list of officers at the Pale RKM. First, can you please confirm for us that this document refers to the officers at the Pale rear command post of the 2nd Military District in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have memorised some of the family names. There is no reason not to believe that this is an accurate list, that was a forward command post in the tourist hotel at Pale. I arrived there --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- towards the evening of 22nd April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please listen to my questions carefully. I'm going to try to go orderly and efficiently and ask you very precise questions. We see it was called a Pale RKM. The RKM stands for rear command post; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reserve command post is also a forward command post, but later on during the war the tourist hotel was used as a rear facility --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- I'm going to go orderly here.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was not the case at the time. That was not a rear facility at the time, only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You were assigned this command post between the 22nd and the 30th of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These were the officers you were assigned to the command post with; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were already there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the third name on the list, it is Branko Filipovic. Is it correct that Branko Filipovic was in charge of the operations staff at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Branko Filipovic. He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P03795 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you is a 6 April 1992, 2nd Military District RKM operations record from Branko Filipovic. The first paragraph states: "The overall activity of this part of the Command has focused primarily on monitoring the situation in the course of ... operations in and around Sarajevo. In addition, we have continued to work on troop deployments and we have organised communications." Does this report accurately represent the responsibilities of the officers at the Pale RKM in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on it. I arrived on the 22nd of April. By nature of things, a larger operational command must have a reserve command post. The main leader of that team was Colonel Brano Filipovic. All I can tell you is that while I was there between the 22nd and the 30th, reports were coming in about operations all over Bosnia aimed against JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to go orderly here.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so -- before we get into different topics, were you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could perhaps clarify one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The English translation has a word that is not in the B/C/S original. This document does not mention troop deployments. The deployments are in relation to communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Work on deployments. I will have it checked but I see that there is maybe a notation that's added there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, apparently you wanted to seek confirmation or denial that this was an accurate description. The witness said, I can't say because, but for the last ten days of April it might be that he could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. That's what -- Your Honour, that was my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, were you personally involved in any of the activities that are described in this document once you arrived at the Pale RKM?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Furthermore, the team there didn't take me seriously, my being a naval officer. They didn't give me any tasks or assignments. I was just sitting and listening to briefings without any participation in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Toward the end of this report, it states: "We have maintained constant contact and coordination of operations with the Pale Crisis Staff." Were you aware of this coordination of operations with the Pale Crisis Staff during your time at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent eight days there. Crisis Staffs existed in every municipality which is according to the law. Obviously, the naval district tried to reduce as much as possible the scope of any combat operations between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which -- I'm stopping you again. Would you please answer to questions rather than to tell us whatever comes to your mind. The question simply was whether you were aware of coordination of operations with the Pale Crisis Staff during your time at the command post. Were you or were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 11089 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up will be a 6 January 2000 "Nin" magazine article entitle: "My Truth." This was previously shown to you during your testimony in the Karadzic case. The article contains an interview provided by General Kukanjac, the former commander of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: While we're turning to that, sir, do you recall being asked about this article in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being asked about this, although I personally know Kukanjac. I spent three days with him at the command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether you remember to have been questioned about it. Not whether you knew Mr. Kukanjac personally. I really have to again stress --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I have to stress that you shouldn't interrupt me. But second, you are at risk that your testimony, which is given and you are called as a witness by the Defence, that you are at risk to affect the probative value by not answering questions. Could you please keep that in mind. It's important for the Defence. It's important for the Chamber to hear answers to questions rather than other matters. Mr. Weber, you have got an answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, then I'll go -- I'll go back through it with you. I'd like to direct your attention to subparagraph (d) which is in the middle of the page before you. This paragraph is in the part of the article where General Kukanjac is discussing what he did since the beginning of 1992. In this paragraph General Kukanjac states: "When we realised what was being done and what was going to happen, we began to pull out the entire mobile assets of the JNA in a timely manner; in an endeavour by both officers and soldiers, employing perfect organisation, we managed to pull out, preserve, and retain everything; even if there had been cases of seizure by the enemy, we would immediately make it up manifoldly; the Muslim-Croat horde never got hold of a single plane, helicopter, tank, armoured personnel carrier, gun, mortar, motor vehicle ...," and then there is an ellipse. Do you see this portion of the article?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I put it to you that this information contradicts your evidence relating to the weaponry left behind for the ABiH, and specifically what you say in paragraph 66 of your statement which is that: "JNA weapons stayed in the Viktor Bubanj, Marshal Tito, 2nd Military District command, and Jusuf Dzonlic barracks." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this article into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11089 receives number P6816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Witness, could I ask you about this same paragraph. You said JNA weapons stayed in all these barracks including heavy weapons. Could you be a bit more precise. What heavy weapons stayed in the Viktor Bubanj, Marshal Tito, and the Jusuf Dzonlic command posts or barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say explicitly that things stayed there, but they did. I don't know how much. I don't know what quota [indiscernible]. As for what I stated, I base that on my stay at the corps. I learned that from operative organs and the activities in Sarajevo that were -- [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you where you learned it. First of all, I read your statement: "JNA weapons stayed in all these barracks including heavy weapons ..." So that you didn't say that they stayed there is at least not in line with your written statement. My question simply was: Including heavy weapons, what heavy weapons if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that they had 105-millimetre howitzers as well as two or three tanks. I don't know any further details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, they stayed in these barracks, if I understand you well, or is it that you say, We later learned that they had these available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principles, those stayed there and then there was activities which proved that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, nothing stays anywhere in principle. Either something stays somewhere or it doesn't stay somewhere. Do you mean to say that you have no exact knowledge about it but that you assume or that you conclude that they must have stayed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I conclude that the Marshal Tito and other barracks were abandoned and they -- the people simply ran from those and that they left combat assets behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You concluded that. You have no personal knowledge, no personal observation of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. It's time for a break. We take a break, Mr. Maksimovic. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, perhaps needless to say but the portion you put to the witness and suggested to him that there was a contradiction, there is not necessarily a contradiction between the two because if General Kukanjac says something about even if there had been cases of seizure, it -- what the witness said does not exclude that these were those cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now we have heard his later answers about his knowledge about the matter, so there's no need. But please be careful in suggesting or putting to a witness that there is a contradiction when the text does not fully justify such a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand what Your Honour is saying and thank you. I'm actually -- based on Your Honour's questions, I'll move to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I was going to follow up on that with P4946 just so the Chamber has the record which would further provide information on that. So it was going to be a segue, but Your Honour established a lack of personal knowledge, so I'm not going to further explore the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. It was also a more general --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- observation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, I'm going to change topics with you now and I want to discuss a figure you mention in paragraph 7 of your statement. In your statement you state that the SRK had about 22.000 men. Is it your evidence that the SRK never had more than 22.000 men between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is indeed my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31413 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a comparative review of changes in strength of the SRK for the period of 4 April to 31 December, 1992, with updated information as of 24 February, 1993. Before we discuss some of the details in the document, do you recognise the units that are mentioned in this review under the name of unit column?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way to enlarge it for the witness so that we only have the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these are some figures which surpass mine, but I guarantee that the 22.000 who were armed, that's what I had in mind. This is everybody, even the auxiliary personnel. They were all members of the corps. In operative terms, there were only 22.000 troops and of those only 12.000 fighters one could rely on. If you reduce the figure even further and if you select from those --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about some of the formations in here. I was just wondering if you recognised the units mentioned. Just so that we make sure that we have a common understanding of the document, I just want you to focus quickly on number 12 which refers to the first Rpbr with what appears to be a full strength of 6.043. And then according to my math, if you subtract the killed and wounded soldiers, a current strength of 5.254. Do you see that information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you -- Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat? Something about 6.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could have the centre of the document enlarged for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is asking you to repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then I was just making sure that he could see it. If we could please have the centre of the document further enlarged for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to follow across --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The centre of the document should be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Potentially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Especially line 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, what I was referring to, it appears according to this report that the 1st Rpbr has a total, a full strength, according to this document, of 6.043 which we see, if you read across to the right, on -- on the line, is there. And then there is a number of 193 and -- related to the number of killed members of that brigade. And 596 for the wounded members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then if we could please scroll over to the right a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see that there -- in the last column, which is entitled "The Current Strength," there is a number of 5.254. Do you see this information?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the date? When was this recorded? Was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of the table? What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could -- I read it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But if we could then zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What this review indicates is that it's for the period of 4 April to 31 December, 1992, and then right underneath that you can see that it's updated with current information from 24 February, 1993. So it would be our position that that final column to the far right would reflect the number based on the current information as of the 24th of February, 1993. Sir, do you understand that that -- that's how this document reads? Just before discussing it with you, I just want to make sure that we are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document contains some parts of the former JNA. If we are talking about the 4th of April, 1992, they were deployed in the logistics base. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is astonishing. What I'm reading is astonishing. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the actual strength as the document appears to be present is the 24th of February, 1993. Wait for a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You understand how the table is structured. Wait for the question Mr. Weber will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we have clarification, is it correct that the 1st Romanija Brigade, Light Infantry Brigade was the largest SRK brigade which is reflected in this document with the highest totals of personnel?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't deal with numbers. That was at the beginning of the war. Later the number was reduced and that's why I said 22.000. It is possible that it was that many but not all of those were operative members of the staff. A lot were auxiliary personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say "operative," do you mean active members of the military as opposed to reserves?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That includes reserves. Nobody was active there. They were all reservists. It was a people's army. None of them were 22-year-old recruits. They were troops ranging in age from 20 to 60. And for your information, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... ^ 10589 2.30.07

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We've heard a lot of information about these things so I'm not going to dwell too much on it. I just -- want to just direct your attention to lines 16 to 18.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could scroll over to the left for the witness a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see that there is reference to the Rajlovac, Vogosca, and Kosevo Brigades. We'll talk about these brigades some more a little bit later, but right now while we're on this document, is it correct that these three brigades joined together and became part of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade when it was formed in early 1994?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they all became the 3rd Vogosca Brigade. The Rajlovac and Kosevo Brigade, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. They were united into another third brigade because both the Rajlovac and Vogosca had less men than a brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, none asked you why it was. Mr. Weber was just seeking whether they were joined in the third brigade. You've answered that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31413 receives number P6817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that individuals were mobilised into the SRK during the early months of the war?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that individuals were mobilised into the Sarajevo Romanija Corps during the early months of the war?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question because I have to respect the Chamber's request. I was not present when those things were done, so I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on to something else then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31430 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you will be appearing a 28 May, 1992, order from SRK commander Tomislav Sipcic related to the training of young soldiers. Under item 1, the order states: "All Corps units are to assemble mobilised young men who have still not done military service and send them to Pale municipality to undergo training lasting 30 days." At the end of the paragraph, the order states: "After the 30-day training, the young soldiers will be sent to combat arms units, where they will continue their specialist training in order to be trained for combat specialities." As a member of the corps command at the time, can you tell us what type of specialist training was provided for these individuals after their initial training in Pale?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never spoke to Sipcic. I never communicated with him. At that time I was in Sokolac and I assisted Lieutenant-Colonel Bosanac in establishing a brigade in Sokolac, so I wouldn't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, is your answer that you do not know what kind of specialist training was provided for these individuals that had been after their initial training? You do not know or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what training it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in handling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then answer that question because that was the question. What was the specialist training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was actually basic training in using basic armament; i.e., rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that after the 30-day training that what is described here as specialist training, is that when they learned how to handle a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the training. And then after that people are ear-marked for various specialties as signalsmen, as mortar crew members, and so on and so forth. That's how things should have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's where they got specialist training on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basic, yes. Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, if I could make a go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in the initial training, did everyone receive -- when they joined the SRK, did they receive what you are describing to be basic training?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was recruited had to undergo that to be made usable. Can I add something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is this what you are referring to as basic training? Just so we can have some idea of what you're discussing.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about young lads who had not served in the army before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, before explanations, I'm just trying to figure out for the record is this what you're referring to as basic training? What everyone went through when they joined.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the basic training was accelerated and those who had never held a rifle in their hands before - I'm talking about young lads - had to undergo that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's pause here for a second and just go step by step. As part of this basic training when they learned to handle rifles, would they be taught marksmanship with those rifles? How to fire those rifles with accuracy.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's routine training. There was fire practice, targets, firing in order to dispel fear of arms in rukez ^ c. There is nothing specialist about that. This is basic training where they are taught how to defend themselves from an attack and how to respond to an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you again and please just focus on my question: Now, were you aware that at this time that the SRK, as part of its rifles, possessed M48 and M76 rifles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, it seems that you're very busy reading rather than listening to the question. The SRK, part of its rifles, did they possess M48s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of them were M48s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is yes. Did they possess M76 rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course they had those as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question please, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, would people be -- receive training on these M48 and M76 rifles as a part of the basic training or would that come after?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about this training. I told you that people were recruited and then whatever follows. And as for the pace of training, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- process of training, I was not in charge. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, during the first basic training, did newly recruited soldiers learn how to fire M48s and/or M76 rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they underwent that training. It all depended on what weapons they were given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Next question please, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your statement, you claim that "the level of training at the SRK can be called lack of training." Sir, it actually seems that you have awareness of the fact that there was training that was offered from the very outset of the war. I put it to you that this contradicts the evidence or at least the portrayal of how you've depicted it in your statement. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have comment. The contingent that was trained, they were -- it was a small number of people. I don't know how many. Perhaps across the entire corps, perhaps several hundred men were trained. As for the rest, those were mostly people who had served in the former JNA. They didn't undergo any training. They were poorly trained. They could only fire a bullet if somebody opened fire at them and to defend themselves in that way. That's why I said that there was a general lack of training across the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just put the question to him for the sake of putting our case to him, so the Prosecution would tender 31430 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31430 receives number P6818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to go through a little bit of your positions to hopefully provide some clarity on this. Is it correct that you were assigned to the morale and information sector of the 2nd Military District between the 30th of April and 15th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday you testified, and this is at transcript pages 26756 to -57 that you first met General Mladic at his request on 15 May, 1992, and that he referred you to General Gvero after you had introduced yourself. Do you know why General Mladic sent you to General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, the 2nd Army District was no longer. When I was released from hotel Europa, I came to Pale, I was at the forward command post, and I was invited to report to Crna Rijeka to General Mladic on the 14th of May. I told you about our encounter yesterday. And then he referred me to General Gvero because he was the assistant for morale in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After you saw General Mladic, did General Gvero give you a further assignment; and more specifically, your assignment to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, the atmosphere was very heavy because of the events in Tuzla and Brcanska Malo [phoen]. The first thing that Gvero ordered me to do ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could answer my question, did General Gvero give you a further assignment to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? Just a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. At that time, was it your understanding -- or actually, where did he assign you at that time? Or did he provide you with an assignment? I guess I'm ahead of myself.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assignments are made according to the will of the commander. On the 24th of May or the 23rd, I went to help Lieutenant-Colonel Bosanac in setting up a brigade at Sokolac to be his assistant and to participate in the forming of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Does that have anything to do with any of your encounters with either General Mladic on General Gvero on the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, General Gvero was acting probably on orders of General Mladic when he told me to go there. I accepted that and I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of your official assignment, is it correct that you served as part of the morale guidance, religious, and legal affairs sector of the SRK command between 15 May and 22 June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Was your superior during this time Colonel Ljuban Kosovac?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo did not issue any orders to me. I -- or immediately went to Ilidza on the north-westerly axis and I remained there until my departure for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- we -- just so we're clear, this is just between the period of 15 May and 22 June, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that you were assigned to the military history institute of the VJ General Staff administration for information and morale guidance between 28 July, 1992, and 1 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was working at the institute. No. I returned to my former position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that -- just so we're clear, I'm saying that you did work for the military history institute during this period, and was that the military history institute of the VJ General Staff administration for information and moral guidance?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of your statement, you indicate that you returned to the SRK on 1 April, 1993. Upon your return, were you assigned to the SRK command sector for moral, religious, and legal affairs? That's the sector you were assigned to; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During this time, is it correct that you were subordinate to Colonel Kosovac, who was the assistant commander for moral, religious, and legal affairs at the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And thank you, sir. I appreciate those clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31433 for the witness. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a -- what I'd like to discuss with you, actually, just so you understand the topic, a little bit further, the tasks of your department and the SRK. Before you is a plan of moral guidance and psychological activities and informing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if we could actually go to the last page in both versions, quickly. And if we could enlarge the very lower right corner, the signature area in the B/C/S version for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to the lower right, can you confirm that this is the signature of Colonel Kosovac?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is his signature. I do not know it, though. But I think it is his signature. I have never seen it, therefore I cannot memorise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You recognise the stamp of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that this is the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand what the stamp says --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never looked carefully at any stamp, so I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's go through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please return to the first page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item 1 of this plan entitled, "Moral and Informing," the plan lists as a permanent task --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I believe that's now cut off for the witness in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As a permanent task: "Present the objectives of defence and the liberation struggle adopted by the RS state and political leadership." Was this one of your tasks? And I just see the --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As a permanent task, it says: "Present the objectives of defence and the liberation struggle adopted by the RS state and political leadership." Was this one of your tasks, to present these objectives?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. Let me just look at the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, let me know when you're ready for me to continue.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We see that the plan lists news agencies as one of the cooperating bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could scroll over a little bit to the right for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this mean that these objectives were intended to be presented through the media?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any specific contacts with the media. That was not done at our level. That was more at the level of the Main Staff and the civilian authorities. Our exclusive scope of work involved only the corps in direct communication with the men who were manning the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you know if the objectives being referred to here, and that's the objectives of defence and the liberation struggle, if they were presented at all through the media with statements emphasising how the VRS is defending the endangered position of the Serbian people in age-old Serbian lands and things of that such?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not done at the corps level but rather at a higher level, so there is nothing disputable about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And that's how the -- the Main Staff level presented these objectives; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember what the Main Staff used to say or tell. I cannot comment on that because I was not aware of what was the Main Staff doing and how the civilian authorities at the republican level were operating in terms of disseminating information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, just so you understand my position on this, it appears according to this document that the responsible -- who's from -- it's from your superior. It appears to indicate that the responsible body for this is the SRK command. So it would be our position that the command of the SRK was also involved in this, just so you understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the last page of both versions. And if we could assist the witness by focusing on item 2 on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item 2 there is another permanent task which, according to this, the responsible body is the organ for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs in the SRK and the units. The permanent task that's listed here states: "Through systemic spreading of misinformation in the media, cover up our real intentions and instigate conflicts and dissent among the enemy's ranks and the ranks of the enemy's supporters." Is it correct that one of the tasks of your organ was to systematically use the media to spread misinformation that covered up the real intentions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I am starting to doubt this document because this is all new to me. Now this item that speaks about religious activities. I never met any of the priests during the war. And as for these other entries, I cannot confirm it. As I said, I am becoming suspicious about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you haven't answered my question. Was this one of your tasks, to spread misinformation in the media?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have any explanation, Witness, as to why this document says that this is a task for the organ for moral, guidance, religious, and legal affairs in the SRK, whereas you say it was not -- at least not part of your task? Do you have any explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure I can do that. This is the first time that I'm seeing this document describing these activities. My official title was assistant commander of the corps for moral guidance; however, my main duty was to offer assistance on the north-westerly axis. Therefore, I wasn't very much involved in these activities but rather in the activities of patching up gaps in the establishment that occurred. In other words, I wasn't very much involved in all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I see that you are saying that this was not what you were tasked with. Were you aware of others performing a task as described here within the organ for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you that the organ for morale of the SRK was rather inert and passive. They didn't do much in that area. And, Mr. President, as I told you, the very fact that people were defending their own home ground, their families, was quite sufficient. We didn't need anyone to boost our morales further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand your answer to be that you are not aware of anyone in your organ for moral, guidance, religious, and legal affairs of the SRK to be involved in the performance of such a task?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, could I ask a follow-up question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic is on his feet, so I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The document was tendered. I'm waiting to object to the document based upon the witness's suspicions raised about the document, his inability to confirm the content of the document and his inability to confirm the signature on the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, so you're aware, this document comes from the archives in the Kozara military barracks in Banja Luka. And it's our position that it is authentic. Before I ask you something related to that, is it correct that you attended the morning meetings of the corps command?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in most cases. Whenever I was in Lukavica, the general would invite me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And you've already said that Colonel Kosovac was your superior. I put it to you that you're purposefully distancing yourself from knowledge in this document because it is unfavourable to the sector that you were a part of. Do you have any other comment?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right. I have no ill-intentions. I made a declaration to speak the truth. However, if there is something dubitable, I cannot confirm it either in a positive or a negative way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would again tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one further question. You said you expressed some doubts of the document. Could you tell us what your doubts are apart from the content which we have discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Due to its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of its --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially the entry relating to religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's content rather than the format or the appearance of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I just have a minute to tell you something? Sometimes there are some sentences which are rather for the sake of formality. You know that an impression is made that there was some religious impact. However, in practice there was very low intensity of these activities. This was more for the sake of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
