utterances.text: We are discussing at this moment the document, not whether the tasks as described in this document were performed or achieved. That's a different matter. Mr. Weber, the document apparently is an attachment number 6 to another document. Do you know what it is related to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. And if I could have a second here. I believe it's related to the plan of moral and psychological activities and informing of the -- if I could just have one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. It was the document I thought it was. We've also uploaded the report that it was a part of, 65 ter 31435. We'd be happy to tender both of the documents into evidence. There is some of the language reflected in this, the other report, which was drafted by Colonel Kosovac and approved by General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it's fine that you give me a number. But that, of course, doesn't tell me much about, apart from that it's attached to another document which has a number. That's what it tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The other document is the plan of moral and psychological activities and informing of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and it was -- I have it down as signed being by Colonel Kosovac and approved by General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then does it have a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The plan is actually undated. But based on the individuals that are assigned, basically Colonel Kosovac, it would be our position that it's sometime in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that on the screen, 65 ter 31435?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now this plan apparently is -- what we see on our screen now is an attachment number 6 to something else as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah. I see that it's part of what is listed as Drina, and I believe, if my recollection serves me right, I can confirm further over the next recess, but there was a whole series of attachments to the Drina materials and there were multiple attachments. So this civic attachment that I'm bringing up is the attachment number 6, which is the plan related to moral and psychological activities and informing of the SRK and the attached list, because that was the topic that I was going to go into with the witness since it pertained to his sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Ivetic, you said it was about the doubts of the witness. We know more about what kind of doubts the witness has. The witness doesn't know the document, so that is clear that we could not deal with it as introduced in, I would say, the traditional way by the witness. At the same time, the witness gave evidence about matters that are described in the document. Is there any objection against admission in more general terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, under what bases? What is the bases for admission? What is the rule or the bases for admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the rule is -- the rule is -- I believe we have had that about 50 or 60 times, that the witness gives evidence about matters which are directly related to what we find in documents. And under those circumstances, I think we deviated from a kind of general rule that bar table documents should be combined. And that's the basis -- would be the basis for admission, I take it, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I am -- as a member of the corps command, I am also offering this to go to his credibility. So he's denied it and he hasn't confirmed things, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the kind of objections Mr. Ivetic refers to and the purpose --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of admitting the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Purpose is not the same of admissibility in itself which is about relevance of probative value and that is not something invoked by Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Responding only to the issue of the bar table submission of document. Your Honours have now said that you have deviated from a rule. I am operating under guidance that Your Honour has issued as to when the Prosecution was to make final bar table submissions of documents. If the document is being presented for the truth of the matter asserted in the document, I submit it is improper to do it through a witness who has no personal knowledge about the document and then to say it is a bar table submission. The time for such submissions has passed and we need to know the entirety of the case that the Defence must answer of the Prosecution. We cannot be constantly adding to the Prosecution's case when it suit the Prosecution during the Defence case. We don't know how to deal with these documents. We relied upon the guidance of the Chamber when the final bar table submissions of the Prosecution would be and what case we would have to answer in our Defence case, and now we're being surprised with new documents at every turn with every witness. As you've said, this has happened 50 or so times. I don't think it has been 50, but it has happened a number of times with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently it escaped your attention what the reasons were for the Chamber not to make those part of general bar table submissions but rather admit them in the context of a testimony of a witness. The objection is denied. Madam Registrar, let me just see whether you have given a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I don't know if you want one or both of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we were discussing the original document. That objection is denied. Now -- yes, then let me just see. That was, Madam Registrar, was number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 31433.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P6819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6819 is admitted into evidence. The reasons for the denial of the objection, Mr. Weber, for the document which is on our screen now, do not apply. I hope that you're aware of that because you've not asked any question about the content of this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I -- I would just leave it to your discretion and

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Microphone, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was only seeking to tender the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I was just leaving it to your discretion whether you wanted the second one or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not tendering it? That's what I establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's time for the break and my client had sent a message asking for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break now, then. Mr. Maksimovic, we would like to see you back in 20 minutes. We resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ivetic, there seems to be a confusion now and then about the admission of documents. When I used the word "bar table" as an other option, I perhaps have not been very clear in my language. Perhaps I should have talked about the admission of a document not through someone who is, has personal knowledge about that document or is familiar with it already or -- and that, of course, would include the author of a document, but rather speak about that category than bar table because bar table is the avenue through which the document is introduced whereas the category I was referring to was of a different kind. It's not an avenue through which but it is about the relation of the document with the testimony given by a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the Chamber will come with some further explanation on this soon so that we avoid any confusion in the near future.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I provide some further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to make sure that there was an accurate statement concerning the list that I just tendered that was an attachment. During the break - and this is P6819 -- during the break I was able to acquire further information. It's part of a register of documents from the SRK corps -- well, the corps, delivered to the Main Staff of the VRS, and we have the cover for it which is dated the 2nd of February, 1994, and these were two of the -- what was shown and admitted was one of the attachments and then the second document was also one of those attachments. So I just wanted to give that to the Chamber so that it was informed of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. You may continue, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, I would now like to switch topics with you and discuss someone who you have previously testified about. Is it correct that you are familiar with Slavko Aleksic? At this time I am simply asking yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Slavko Aleksic never undertook anything on his own initiative without the knowledge of the SRK command; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Slavko --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Slavko Aleksic acted exclusively pursuant to orders passed through the SRK chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that the manner in which these questions are being asked calls for specification. Without talking about specific, concrete acts or specific, concrete circumstances where in these statements might have been said, the simple assertion in a very generic and vague manner about an individual I believe is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two. To some extent, I do agree with you, Mr. Ivetic. First of all, Mr. Weber, the answer to the first question is most likely not reliable and that relates to the question because whether Slavko Aleksic never undertook anything of his own initiative without the knowledge of the SRK command, you mean to say in a professional context which, of course, is not part of the question. I may take it that he has gone into town and buy a bread without the previous. Therefore, and that is the second issue, and I tend to agree with Mr. Ivetic, if you ask him whether the witness is aware of any occasion where Slavko Aleksic undertook anything on his own initiative without the knowledge of the SRK command, then you have phrased the question in such a way that the answer is -- and then still in his professional capacity I would say because the witness may be familiar with the acts and conduct of Mr. -- of the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on a private level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's just a matter of phrase it in such way that you avoid any of the comments rightly --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put by Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will do this another way. I was trying to be expedient and just confirm previous things I'd stated. Could the Prosecution have 65 ter 31442, page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, is it correct that you previously -- well, I'll just go through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, during the Karadzic proceedings you were asked about a quotation from actually the Seselj case and something Mr. Seselj said during his proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then going to -- going to line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The question that was posed to you in the Karadzic case was: "And just with regard to the content of that statement, I'd like to read to you from page 8673 of the transcript in the Seselj proceedings something that Dr. -- or Mr. Seselj quoted, and I'd like to ask if you can confirm that. He says, starting at line 6, that you wrote, referring to you: "'Aleksic never undertook anything of his own initiate or without the knowledge of the corps command. He acted exclusively pursuant to orders.'" You were then asked: "Can you confirm that that's what you set out in your statement from Mr. Seselj." Your answer was: "I can confirm that because that was also the opinion of the corps command" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. And if I can have the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we need only one version because there is no B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next page doesn't seem to say what you were saying, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I think we're on a different page. I'm looking for 31578 which should be page 20 of this upload. And as I'm continuing reading here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your answer was, starting at line 2 here: "I can confirm that, because that was also the opinion of the corps command, that he did not do anything. He just defended his small area of responsibility very difficult and very dangerous, the Jewish Cemetery." Do you stand by this evidence?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution now have 65 ter 30852.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I do want to discuss a little further with you Mr. Aleksic in relation to this document. This -- coming up before you will be a 16 December, 1993, request for ammunition from Slavko Aleksic. According to the document, he was the commander of the anti-tank company of the Jewish Cemetery. Were you aware that Mr. Aleksic held this position as part of this company?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you how I met Aleksic. When I arrived in the corps, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You must answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Correct. He was in charge of anti-tank combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The document indicates that it was sent to a battalion commander by the name of Blagoje Kovacevic. Is it correct that Blagoje Kovacevic was actually the brigade commander of the 1st Smbr at this time in 1993? I'm just asking you this for clarification purposes.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: December 1993.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Stojanovic was commander that year. Aleksic had a low rank. Later on he was in the Igman Brigade or Blazuj Brigade. I can't confirm about Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the zone of responsibility at the time in the Jewish Cemetery, is it correct that that was in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Smbr, the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was within the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, and I just remembered that Kovacevic was the commander of the battalion. He was not in direct -- he was in direct contact with Aleksic because Aleksic was a member of that battalion. Now we have clarified that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to further explore what other detail knowledge that you have regarding this company with this document. And if you could look over the types of ammunition being requested. Were you aware that Mr. Aleksic's company possessed weaponry for this type of ammunition? So if you could take your time, look at the list, and then let me know what your answer to your question -- my question is.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is ammunition for infantry defence. He had a very small area in the Jewish Cemetery. 7.62, 7.9. Yes, that's the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, whether he was aware. Because I'd like to know -- because you're made a very general statement about Mr. Aleksic. We do have further details, so I'm just probing the depth of your knowledge, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even -- Mr. Weber, your question was whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- whether you were aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the company possessed weaponry for this type of ammunition, and then the witness said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- this was ammunition for infantry defence but he has not told us whether weaponry, in which this ammunition fits in, whether that was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't want to -- if you want to skip that question, fine, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not there yet, Your Honour. I believe that page 58, line 3, my question was actually phrased "were you are aware," so I was first seeking to confirm what the witness's level of awareness was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So were you aware that Mr. Aleksic's company possessed this ammunition? Or possessed weaponry for this type of ammunition that we see here?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure about all of the ammunition. I'm just aware of the calibre 7 and 12.7 to the ordinal number 7, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when you're saying that you're aware of that, you're aware that there was rifles that could fire that type of ammunition that was in the possession of this company?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they had. I toured those positions only once. When I provided a statement for Aleksic, I had consulted with Colonel Lugonja and asked him whether he had acted on the orders of the command and he confirmed that he did. He was very disciplined when it came to combat operations in Grbavica. I'm talking about Aleksic. So he was under the strict command of the corps and he obeyed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did Colonel Lugonja tell you this?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were in charge of the Seselj Defence asked me if I could say something about Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I told them --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was asking you, you just mentioned that Colonel Lugonja provided you information concerning Mr. Aleksic. When did he tell you this?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I drafted a statement for Aleksic. Lugonja was a very well informed man. The best informed man in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you give me year?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did Mr. Lugonja tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. Ten years ago, when we talked when I drafted that statement. That wasn't something I would try to remember because I thought it was a matter of routine. I put some questions to him. He read what I wrote. He confirmed that everything was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you present that in your statement as information by Mr. Lugonja or did you present that in your statement as information from yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just told you. I consulted with Lugonja. I read one page to him and he agreed with everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've heard that and that caused me to put this question to you. Did you in your statement say, "This is what Mr. Lugonja told me and I'm presenting it as such to you," or did you present it as your own knowledge? Is the statement available, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could you please answer my question, whether -- how you presented that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed that statement with full Lugonja's consent. The text, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. Mr. Ivetic, we slowly are coming to a point where the Chamber has to consider whether or not it makes any sense to continue this examination where the witness on numerous occasions again and again and again is not answering questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour. And I think Your Honour is taking a position that is unfair. And I ask Your Honour to consider the question that you asked and the answer that you received when you asked just now, if I can go back, at line 19 through 20: "Did you in your statement say, 'This is what Mr. Lugonja told me and I'm presenting it as such to you,' or did you present it as to your knowledge?" And then you ask, "Is the statement available ..." Could you please answer my question how you present it. And he said, "I signed that statement with full Lugonja's consent," which is not a perfect translation of what was said in Serbian. But, in any event, he said he signed the statement with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course I was talking about presenting it as far as the content is concerned and not as far as signatures are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which you can follow up with, but to present it as the witness is not answering your question, I believe, is a severe -- is a more drastic interpretation of what the witness actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Look at page 60, line 15, where I explained to the witness quite clearly what I meant by presenting, whether he said, This is what Mr. Lugonja told me or, This is what I -- in the statement. And I am -- I have taken notice of your observations, Mr. Ivetic, and so has the Chamber, and I would remind Mr. Mladic that he should not speak aloud. I have a few questions. The statement for Mr. Aleksic, Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, if you speak aloud again, you know what the consequences will be. If there is any problem with the translation? Apparently there is. Mr. Mladic apparently does not receive interpretation. Mr. Ivetic, the reference I just gave was a wrong one. The line, I think you should focus on, is page 60, lines 18, 19, and 20, where I further explained what I meant with how it was presented. I leave it to that for the time being. I just correct my reference. Has the problem with the audio been resolved? It has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It totally has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can continue. Yes. I was asking you, Witness, that statement for Mr. Aleksic, in what context did you prepare that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His people. People who were in charge of his Defence. They asked me to do that in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was that statement, as far as you're aware of, ever used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is any of the parties aware of any statement given by this witness in relation to Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the core of our initial awareness was based on what Mr. Seselj said during his case and how he represented it, so then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Likewise from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Likewise from the Defence. The only reference is the reference in the transcript to where it was read in the Karadzic case referring to the Seselj case. I've not seen a physical statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we don't have that available. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But nonetheless, maybe we can -- can I just ask a few questions here. Sir, you drafted the statement and you showed it to Colonel Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And having done that, you then signed it as your own statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just to make it clear, in your statement you didn't refer to Colonel Lugonja, you just submitted it as your own statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I signed it. But I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I tender the document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30852 receives number P6820, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the next topic I'm going to explore something that -- could I go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you were ordered to report to the Vogosca tactical group on 11 July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were ordered to the Vogosca tactical group two days after it was formed; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was it shortly after its formation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was summer time and that General Galic asked me to go up there to provide assistance because they had a shortage of manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The commander of the Vogosca tactical group was Dragan Josipovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As of July 1993, you were subordinated to Dragan Josipovic of the Vogosca tactical group command; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was, however, a temporary strength or composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, is it correct that for that temporary assignment, and we understand that tactical groups are temporary in their formation, is it correct that you were part of the command staff of the Vogosca tactical group?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: General Galic came to visit the command of the Vogosca tactical group two or three times per month; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking if it was a rule. I'm asking if that is what occurred. Is it correct that General Galic came to visit the command of the Vogosca tactical group two to three times per month?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never happened that he would come two or three times a month. He would come whenever he felt it was convenient or appropriate for him to come, but it was never three times in a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, during your time there, approximately how many times per month do you recall him coming to visit?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not come specifically to Vogosca. Whenever he came, he would visit Ilijas, Hadzici, and other places, the whole area. I cannot tell you exactly. He came according to his own schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if we can make this shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But, unfortunately, Your Honours, I need to return into private session for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the units subordinated to the Vogosca tactical group were the Vogosca Brigade, the Ilijas Brigade, the Rajlovac Brigade, and the Kosevo Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the zone of responsibility for the Vogosca tactical group extended to the Grdonja feature as part of its eastern border and included a portion of Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The western border of the tactical group's zone of responsibility included Rajlovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31235 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 1 March, 1994, SRK command report from General Galic to the VRS Main Staff. According to the beginning of the report, there was a 5 February order from the VRS Main Staff concerning TG Vogosca, and then General Galic indicates that the Rajlovac, Kosevo, and Vogosca Brigades had been integrated into the 3rd Spbr. Is it correct that the Vogosca tactical group was disbanded in February 1994 when these three brigades were merged into the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Dragan Josipovic was made the commander of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were the deputy commander of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade up until June 1994?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Throughout your statement, you describe various positions you held during this time-period; in particular, I'm referring to paragraphs 4 and 15. Is it correct that you failed to mention that you were the deputy commander of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not forget that. I think I did mention it, mention that. But then again, it was a provisional situation. There was no commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, sir, in paragraph 4 of your statement you say: "Between 1 April, 1993, and 1 September, 1994, I was at the Sarajevo Romanija Corps SRK command." And in paragraph 15, you say: "Due to the lack of command staff as assistant for morale, I was occasionally dispatched in 1993 and 1994 to the north-western front to the Vogosca 3rd Sarajevo Brigade and the Igman Brigade." And then you say where the brigade's zone of responsibility stretch from. So my question was actually very precise. In those paragraphs you do not mention your position and that being that you were the deputy commander of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. Both de facto and de jure, I was in the corps and I was discharging those duties. So that is correct. I discharged those duties in my capacity of a member of the corps staff. However, it was Galic who made all the decisions that were relevant for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber has your statement, so I'm not going to go in circles with you about what is and is not in there. But just for fairness, I'm also going to put to you that you don't mention in your statement that -- your assignment to the command of the Vogosca tactical group. Do you have any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it happened that way, how it went unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on. Is it correct that Miroslav Krajisnik became the assistant commander for morale in the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the report in front of us, General Galic indicates that the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade was formed as an infantry brigade with all elements and units ready to accomplish combat tasks. Is it correct that the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade took over the weaponry and equipment which was previously available to the Rajlovac, Kosevo, and Vogosca Brigades?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't take over anything. Everything was left on the positions, only organisation-wise it was the 3rd Sarajevo. According to its capacity and its numbers, it was below the standard that is applicable to a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You're speaking about qualifications, but I think you've answered my questions for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 65 ter 31235 into evidence. And we note for the record that the 5 February, 1994 -- oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. That the 5 February, 1994, Main Staff order referred to in this document is admitted as P4345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31235 receives number P6821, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever heard of Operation Lukavac 93?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Today at temporary transcript page 7, you stated: "No territories were ever attacked, not even outside of the zone of Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I'm not aware of that." My question to you is: Do you consider that the 546 square kilometres of territory that was liberated by the SRK during the Lukavac 93 operation to be an offensive operation, an offensive action?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a well-thought out operation including the mountainous area between Jahorina and Treskavica in order to achieve a link-up between the territories of Herzegovina and the Romanija plateau. It was a very treacherous terrain for this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you're not answering my question. Just simply, do you consider that to be an offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have -- I'm sorry, it's Exhibit P6549, currently marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is General Galic's 26 June, 1993, order for further operations concerning Operation Lukavac 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask that we actually go directly to page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the English on the right side of our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I was looking for page 3 in both versions. I believe we have it in the B/C/S but not the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention to the first full paragraph after the indentations. The paragraph states: "The goals of the offensive are linking of the majority of our forces ..." I'm not sure actually if this is correct "... compromising of offensive activities of Rajlovac and Vogosca Brigade and possible unblocking of Sarajevo from the direction of Visoko."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the English version be enlarged a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And it's the upper third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, considering your role in the Vogosca tactical group, did you participate as part of the operations Lukavac 93, as part of the -- as part of those operations that came after this order? We see reference to two subordinate brigades of the tactical group, the Rajlovac and Vogosca Brigades.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary task of the tactical group was to defend its zone of responsibility, and it did so parallel with the Lukavac 93 operation. Since there was great danger, General-Colonel Milosevic was there in order to reinforce our defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that this paragraph is -- contradicts what you keep on describing as a defensive, because it clearly says that these are offensive activities, "The goals of the offensive ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you abandoning the question you had asked which was not answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you want the -- yeah -- I'll defer to you on my next question if you'd like the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to know if you are abandoning it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, I think you have kind of answered this in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that these two brigades -- that they were under the Vogosca tactical group as part of these operations, these offensive -- what's described as offensive?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These brigades stayed at their positions. They didn't go anywhere. They were not involved in offensive operations between Jahorina and Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time. Your Honours. I think we're back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a number already. I believe it's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Ms. Stewart just actually reminded me of something important, that was it was MFI'd pending a final CLSS translation which we do not yet have. So if we can just keep that of record then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: MFI should stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's said here that the OTP intended to use this document with another witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm now using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are now using it with another witness but still it's not translated. We'll wait for the translation. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I rise, although I don't know if the -- well, the inference has been made that the witness somehow is -- said that there were no offensive actions. That's not what he said, and I turn to the paragraph 10 of this statement which is actually talking about this precise operation that we have just had cross-examination about where he actually identifies it as being offensive operations. So I think that there has been a little bit of misrepresentations in terms of the actual testimony of this witness on record about this operation which is not at all contradicted by the testimony that we have just heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second please, Mr. Ivetic. Yes, Judge Moloto may have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at this paragraph 10 where from line 2 it says: "During which time it carried out offensive operations ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I thought you were rising on the fact that these were not offensive operations but defensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm mindful -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the Prosecution had intimated that this witness had denied that offensive operations had been undertake by the SRK and the witness's testimony is to the opposite which he has confirmed again today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But I think a lot of this is argument and we're not necessarily spending time on it but the original question related to statement today in court in which he said no territories were ever attacked, not even outside the zone of Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So I was using Lukavac 93 because it's actually the most dramatic example of taking of areas before that, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then we had the follow-up of that in court today where he said no solely Muslim areas were attacked. No exclusively Muslim areas were attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also, to some extent, semantics, whether an attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is always offensive or whether a counterattack we have had that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours have heard a lot of evidence about this operation too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's leave it to that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. I do not have much more. I will finish rather early in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then how much time you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to go to one more document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more document. Mr. Ivetic, how much time you would need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I should be able to finish within ten minutes, eight to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it still could make sense to have the next witness standby. Therefore, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may use the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so the Chamber doesn't think I made up a random figure, I -- in my -- in one of my previous questions, I referred to 546 square kilometres taken during Lukavac 93. The source of this was P4439, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31425.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's P6821 -- I beg your pardon. I'm sorry. I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you is a 14 April, 1994, VRS Main Staff intelligence sector security department report from Colonel Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of the report, Colonel Beara states: "On 12 April, 1994, I was at Sarajevo 3rd Infantry Brigade attending a briefing of the battalion and assistant commanders. The briefing was led by Colonel Maksimovic, the Brigade Chief of Staff. The briefing was also attended by 'Vojvoda' Jovo Ostojic, the commander of the SRS volunteers detachment which came to 3rd Spbr at the end of March." Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting did take place, I'm sure. I remember. But like through a fog.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you recall who attended the meeting besides yourself and Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that the commanders of the brigades were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You sound like you might be guessing. Do you have any clear recollection of individuals who were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember the issues that they had with Ostojic. When they were unarmed, the problem was how to arm them. There were no weapons. We managed to gather some weapons. They were dispatched to their positions. They did not feel safe in their positions. After 25 days I disarmed them and I returned them to where they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true and nothing else. As for the rest --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that this SRS volunteer detachment, when it came to the 3rd Spbr, was under your command since were the chief of staff which correlates to the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were subordinated to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Which included you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, Colonel Beara indicates that you complained to him about Jovo Ostojic and Vukasin Kuzman, aka Pena, a member of the SRS and a former battalion commander at Rajlovac Brigade who blamed you "for not getting the volunteers any automatic weapons, uniforms, and other equipment while they were 'dying for the Serbian people.'" I know you've briefly commented on this so far, but was that -- was that exactly what your complaint was?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kuzman was not the commander of the Rajlovac Battalion. He was the commander of the Krivoglavci, Josenac Brigade. As for Jovo Ostojic, I can't complain of him. I talked to him. He accepted my suggestions. With his help, I managed to send them back. He was listening, he saw that things were not as they should be, and that's why he returned. I had a lot of problems with Kuzman because he is a very arrogant man. He is not up to the responsibility of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- again Mr. Weber read to you what was reported by Mr. Beara. Now, what he read to you, that you had complained to him, is that accurate? Did that happen? Did you not search complaints as read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that I complained because some people did not want me there. Beara did not make things up. He did not invent that complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the way in which he describes your complaints is therefore accurate; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of the paragraph, and this is paragraph -- the second paragraph, Colonel Beara states: "Maksimovic rose above the whole thing and ordered his logistics assistant to equip the volunteer unit." Is it correct that this is what you did: You gave orders to provide weapons to these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We asked for weapons, we found them in the Ilijas and Vogosca Brigade, and we armed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the English version and stay on the same page but at the bottom of the B/C/S. This is the top in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to the last paragraph on the page before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the top of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this paragraph Colonel Beara states: "On 26 March, 95 volunteers came to the brigade and another seven on 11 April. They were given an area around Golo Brdo and Zuc to defend."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It reads "or Zuc."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "Or Zuc." Thank you for the clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your statement you claim that there were 30 unarmed volunteers who came to the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. Is it correct that in fact the number of volunteers that came to the brigade were greater than what you have said so far in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could please turn to P6816, the first page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, while we wait for the document I will tell you this is the article from "Nin" magazine from the year 2000; that is, I guess, a form of an open letter from General Kukanjac which you were asked questions about during the cross-examination. Now, the title of the piece is "My Truth," and then in the first paragraph of both versions, it is explained that General Kukanjac approached the "Nin" editorial board and wanted to repudiate some allegations published in their magazine. And in the preamble to his letter, it states that the allegations as to his name were in 1999. Were you aware of the allegations or criticisms of Kukanjac that would have been circulated in 1999 that he was responding to by way of this open letter?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of any negative comments or besmirches to the reputation of Kukanjac that were circulated following his withdrawal from Sarajevo and from the 2nd Military District of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Military District was disbanded. Kukanjac and I talked in Belgrade on several occasions. He complained about some people in Belgrade. He did it publicly. He said that they did not show support and understanding for his position while he was in Sarajevo. I can't say anything bad about Kukanjac or his attitude towards me or our relationship. He came to where I lived in collective housing on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to then move on. You were asked at temporary page 29 about the number of troops in the SRK, and this was in relation to document P6817. And while we wait for that document, at temporary transcript page 29 you said that the SRK had 22.000 men under arms of which only 12.000 were fighters you could rely on. What exactly did you mean? What kind of distinction were making between the 22.000 and the 12.000 figure?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12.000 that I mentioned were soldiers who were engaged on the lines of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the inner circle bordering on the city. As for the rest of them, that was a semi-combat complement of the military. They were employed in the rear -- in the elements of the rear. Further on, I wanted to say that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was stretched to its outer limits. Unlike the enemy side which had three times as many soldiers and their soldiers were resting for three days since then they would spend one day in the trenches, this means that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was never a danger for Sarajevo. It was never a source of hardship in the city of Sarajevo. And I can also say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the Army of Republika Srpska, including the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, could never have taken Sarajevo because Sarajevo could never have been taken from the low lying land but from the hill tops. All the enemy forces entered Sarajevo from Pale. The Main Staff never undertook any preparations to that effect. Let's sum up. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps was there to protect the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the Serbian substance in Sarajevo field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- you were asked by Mr. Weber whether the distinction between operative and auxiliary troops was a reference to active and reserve officers and you said it was not, but you were not asked to give your definition of what is the difference between an operative and auxiliary troop or soldier. So please tell us, what is the difference between "operative" and "auxiliary" troops?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative units could manoeuvre, could go to different theatres of war, who could be engaged in defence and in attack. And in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, when I say "operative," I mean that they were there to protect the area and territory under the control of Serb forces. Let me give you an example. A modern brigade of the former JNA, in case of a war, it would have crushed the Sarajevo Romanija Corps immediately. A modern brigade had 3- to 4.000 people and was considered a truly operational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if you could define for us what is the core element that defines an auxiliary unit?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Auxiliary units are mainly units of the rear, quartermasters service, technical service. Every brigade has that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now looking at the documents that was presented to you, P6817, here among the various units that are identified and for whom personnel are counted, we see, for instance, the transport battalion number 5, the medical battalion at number 4, the engineering battalion at number 6, the military prosecutors office at number 19, the military court at number 20, and the -- the Han Pijesak RNC at number 11. Would such personnel be considered combat ready troops in military parlance?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we pay so much attention to this? Only a slight difference. 22.000, 20.000 is almost the same, and it becomes clear that -- I mean, that military courts are not the best ones to put at the front, Mr. Ivetic, or even prosecutors. Mr. Weber, it goes without saying. Therefore, I -- Mr. Weber has paid some attention to the accuracy of the number of 20.000, where the document brings us to 22.000 actual serving. I wonder whether we should pay that much attention to these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it was raised by the Prosecution as an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- effort to discredit this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm going through it and we see his explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was not given during the cross-examination when it was suggested that the difference between the operative and auxiliary is active and reserve. So I'm trying to clear the record and give Your Honours the full evidence so that you can know the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the reason why I let you go for a while, but I can tell you that the military courts had caught my eyes already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't necessarily -- I mean, yes. I think, Your Honour, the Prosecution would slightly disagree with the reading of it in terms of your focussing on the current strength, I believe, as of 24th February, 1993. But the column -- the full strength of the RJA which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then you should have asked the witness whether it was ever at full strength and not just -- -

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, the document speaks for ourselves would be our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the statement of the witness does not contradict that because he never said, The full strength, which was not only on paper which we ever had, was 30.000. You should have clarified that, to start with. Let's move on. I think the issue is perfectly clear at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Then I only again would thank Ship-of-the-line Captain Maksimovic for his testimony. That was the last question I had in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Maksimovic, since the Bench has no further -- let me first, Mr. Weber, I had forgotten that you still have a round to go. No questions from the Prosecution. This means that this concludes your evidence, Mr. Maksimovic, and it concludes your testimony, and we would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions and we even noticed that you would even go further and would have told us more, but I take it that you understand that what we should focus on is best defined by the parties and the Chamber always supports that. But it's appreciated that you wanted to give a lot of information. We wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you. Could I be allowed to say goodbye to the general? Maybe it would be a precedent, but I would like to do that and then I will go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact. No, it is -- the accused has heard that you wished to do that. That should do it. It's not common in a court that the witness greets the accused even when he has concluded his testimony. But the accused certainly has heard your request which may mean something to him. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Very well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. Our next witness is Mr. Mile Ujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted -- yes, apparently the Prosecution gets a bit nervous. For what reason, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to note that Mr. Lukic and I had agreed that this particular witness should be informed of his rights under Rule 90(E) before his testimony commences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'll read Rule 90(E) to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just to make some space, if I could ask your permission for Ms. Lee and I to be excused, although it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are. You are excused. Language sometimes is puzzling, to ask for permission to be excused. I take it that the Prosecution intended to ask to be excused. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's accurate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ujic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text is handed out to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Ujic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, in relation to the solemn declaration you have given a second ago, I'd like the draw your attention to the following Rule, and I'll first read it to you: "A witness," that would be you, "may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate that witness himself. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." So if you fear that by giving a truthful answer you might incriminate yourself, please address me and you can ask for not having to answer that question in order to avoid that you would incriminate yourself. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Ujic.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just ask the assistance of the usher so we provide Mr. Ujic with his clean statement. We can show it to the Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as always, it is helpful to ask the witness for his name --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- especially in this case because the name was, I think, not properly reported in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ujic, can you please slowly state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Mile Ujic. I was born on the 25th of May, 1951, in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In front of you, you have a document. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: That's my statement given to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just pause between questions and answers to allow the interpreters to do their job.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see 1D1701 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you say the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We just missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, do you see the signature on the cover page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now go to the last page on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature on this page and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is what is contained in this statement as your account truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it is both truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you essentially give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: I would give the same answers using the same words, let's say, in 99 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1701 receives number D691, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we start, actually, I forgot to ask Your Honours for the extension of direct. We sent e-mails yesterday to the Prosecution and to Your Honours, and we would ask for one hour instead of 30 minutes for direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We certainly have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections. Mr. Lukic, you can proceed. We'll not stop you at the usual 30 minutes. But, of course, it always depends on how it develops. Use your time as efficiently as possible and if you bring good, solid evidence to the Chamber, then we would give you even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope I won't need more. Thank you. First I will read statement summary of this witness and I will proceed with the questions, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have to admit that this statement summary will be a bit longer than its usual, but not too long. Mile Ujic was born on 25th of May, 1951, and lived in Rogatica. Shortly after the multiparty elections in 1990, he was elected president of the Rogatica Executive Board. He was later appointed as department head of the Rogatica Defence Ministry and acting chief of the Rogatica Brigade. According to Mr. Mile Ujic, nationalist provocations began to manifest themselves in early 1991. In June 1991, the Rogatica secretary for national defence mobilised the reserve forces to assist with the crisis. Of the reserve members of the Rogatica Brigade, 60 per cent had been Muslims. However, a great number of Muslims did not respond to the mobilisation and those who were mobilised to Han Pijesak and Zaluzani were later returned by bus at the initiative of the SDA party. While all military-fit Serbs were mobilised into the 216th Brigade, Muslim men filled the reserve police and received weapons. It was clear that from early 1992 onwards there was no unity in Rogatica. Police was divided and then in May 1992, the assembly unanimously voted for the division of Rogatica into Muslim and Serb territories. The war in Rogatica began with the murder of a Serb, Mihaljovic, Drazenko, on the 22nd of May, 1992, after which the Muslims refused to return his body. Following this, the city was not safe to walk around. Many Serb families moved to the countryside and Muslim families move to Sarajevo and Gorazde. Mile Ujic was aware that Muslim extremists burned down many houses of Serbs who had left the town. They also set fire to Serbian bars, a hotel, synagogue, and the power station, leaving Rogatica without electricity for a long time. The Rogatica municipality Serb Territorial Defence warned Muslim citizens to surrender weapons. Some Muslims did surrender weapons and those who did took refuge in a high school together with Serbian and Croatian families and others who were afraid of the war. Most people in Muslim villages were armed and ambushes were often carried out on Serbian civilians using the roads. The Serb Crisis Staff and the Serb Territorial Defence command asked these Muslims to peacefully surrender weapons in exchange for security, but some did not accept this. Those villages who were reluctant to join the conflict surrendered weapons and enjoyed full protection. During the liberation of Rogatica, the Rogatica Brigade suffered losses. This was the statement summary of Mr. Ujic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've got a few more minutes to ask the first questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Ujic, thank you for being patient. We only have a few minutes so let me first ask you something about the army of Muslims in the Rogatica area. Can you please explain to us the position of the chief of police in Rogatica in the wake of multiparty elections and in view of the division of offices within the police in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that. As it was said at the beginning of my statement, following the first multiparty election, I was appointed the president of the Executive Committee that had five members. According to the ratio of population, the power divided --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are invited to speak slower so that the interpreters can follow you. Could you please resume. You said, "According to the ratio of population, the power divided ..." and would you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 60:40 per cent, which means that the Muslims had three members on the Executive Committee, whereas the Serb side had two members, myself and another one. By that logic of majority people, it was the Muslims, the three members of the committee, had the right to choose the departments that they wished. We were given two other departments. One of those departments was the public security station. However, as a rule, at least at the time of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the chief of the police was a Muslim or a Serb, the police station commander would be a member of our other ethnic group. We expected that since they had taken the position of the chief of the police station that we would be given the police commander as a Serb. However, that did not happen. That position was covered by Ramiz Alajbegovic, the former commander of the police station, who was also at the same time in charge of the police reserve force. So this post that we were given in terms of the division of power was as actually not being observed and honoured. So we didn't have any representative in the police. This same person, Ramiz Alajbegovic, recruited members for the police reserve force following the departure of the Serbs. He was left with the Muslim conscript. At the same time, incidentally or not, Muslims returned from training in Croatia and were immediately integrated into the police reserve force. All of them were given weapons, automatic rifles and suchlike. So all of a sudden, the police grew manyfold compared to the one that existed before the war. All of this contributed to increased anxiety among the Serbs who felt endangered and threatened, not only because they were a minority but because many of the conscripts were mobilised for the Han Pijesak Brigade which even increased to the level of minority that we were, and it aggravated the situation even more. It was also difficult for me to work as the president of the Executive Committee because I was under the pressure on the one hand from the Serbs, and on the other hand I wanted to maintain peace in Rogatica at any cost to keep the industry and businesses going. However, there was a saber rattling on a daily basis and that's how it remained throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you went well already beyond the specific question that was asked. We'll conclude the hearing for today. You've been only with us for a quarter of an hour, but we'll resume tomorrow, and we would like to see you back at 9.30 in the morning. You may now follow the usher. But not until after I have instructed you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony that's still to be given. If you understand this, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we adjourn, could I also encourage you to keep a firm hand in keeping the witness close to what you asked the witness about. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, on the 16th of October, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of October, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.
